title: Journalism in Crisis: Independence, Ownership, and the Fight for Truth

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Bekova
dialogue.text: Good morning. I want to talk today about a question that goes to the heart of democratic society: what is the role of journalism, who pays for it, and what happens when those who pay for it have interests in what it reports?

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Bekova
dialogue.text: Let me start with what journalism is, at its best. It is the systematic gathering, verification, and communication of information about matters of public importance. A free press — one that can investigate those in power without fear of legal or commercial retribution — is widely recognised as essential to democratic accountability. When governments abuse power, when corporations pollute communities, when public officials accept bribes — it is typically journalism that exposes these things first. The free press is, in a real sense, one of the foundations of a functioning democracy.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Bekova
dialogue.text: But journalism faces an existential crisis. The business model that sustained quality journalism for most of the twentieth century — advertising revenue from print media — has been largely destroyed by the internet. Digital advertising flows primarily to platforms like Google and Meta, not to news publishers. As a result, newsrooms have been dramatically downsized. Investigative journalism — which requires significant time, resources, and legal expertise — is the most expensive to produce and has been cut most deeply.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Bekova
dialogue.text: This crisis has been exploited by a range of actors. In many countries, local news deserts have emerged — areas in which there is no longer any sustained, professional coverage of local government, local courts, or local public services. Without this watchdog function, local corruption and incompetence go undetected and unchallenged. Research has consistently found that areas without local newspapers show higher levels of local government corruption and lower levels of civic participation.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Bekova
dialogue.text: Media ownership is another critical issue. When news organisations are owned by individuals or corporations with significant business interests in other sectors, the potential for conflicts of interest is obvious. An owner who also runs property developments might be reluctant to cover a story about housing corruption. An owner with close political ties might use their media platform to advance particular political interests. The concentration of media ownership in the hands of a small number of very wealthy individuals is a structural threat to press independence.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Bekova
dialogue.text: What can be done? First, there is a strong case for public funding of journalism — through models like the BBC or the CBC in Canada — that maintain editorial independence while providing a stable funding base. Second, local community news models, supported by philanthropic funding or reader subscriptions, have shown promise in some markets. Third, and perhaps most importantly, citizens need to become active consumers of journalism: subscribing to outlets they value, sharing quality reporting, and recognising that the quality of our information environment is partly a function of the choices we make as readers.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Bekova
dialogue.text: I want to close with something that sounds simple but is easy to forget. Not all news sources are equal. Some are committed to accuracy, independence, and the public interest. Others are committed to entertaining their audience, confirming their biases, or advancing specific political or commercial interests. The difference matters — both for individuals and for societies. The question of which journalism we choose to fund and to trust is, in a real sense, a question about the kind of society we want to live in.
